sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The person or thing that receives the action.
sections.detail: The noun affected by the action of a transitive verb.

sections.heading: When is it used?
sections.text: Use this label for what someone acts on, not simply for any word after a verb.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The letter receives the action of writing.

sections.heading: Related rule
sections.text: The direct object is normally in the accusative state.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The person or thing that performs the action of an active verb.
sections.detail: The grammatical subject of an active verbal clause; it may also experience a state.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Who wrote? The student.

sections.heading: Related rule
sections.text: The subject of the verb is normally nominative.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A verb form usually used for a completed action.
sections.detail: The perfect verb form normally presents an action as completed; its time depends on the context.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The writing is presented as completed.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A verb describing an action happening now, happening regularly, or yet to happen.
sections.detail: The imperfect form can express present, habitual or future actions, depending on context.

sections.heading: How to recognise it
sections.text: It often begins with one of these letters. A prefix alone does not prove that a word is a verb.
sections.arabic: أَ ـ نَ ـ يَ ـ تَ

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Here the verb describes ongoing or regular writing.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: One of the grammatical states a word can have. Direct objects often have this state.
sections.detail: Naṣb is a grammatical state used for several noun functions and for imperfect verbs after certain particles.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The student is the direct object here.

sections.heading: Case marker
sections.text: The ending varies by word type. A fatḥah does not always mean that a word is accusative.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A grammatical state often used for the subject of a verb.
sections.detail: Rafʿ is used for subjects and other functions; its visible marker depends on the word type.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The student is the subject of the verb. Here its ending is a ḍammah; other word types use other markers.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A particle that comes before a noun and puts that noun in the genitive state.
sections.detail: A preposition governs a following noun or attached pronoun.

sections.heading: Preposition
sections.text: This particle means “in”.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The noun follows the preposition, so it is genitive.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A grammatical state used for nouns after prepositions and for the second noun in a possessive construction.
sections.detail: Jarr belongs to nouns; its marker varies by noun type.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The house follows the preposition “in”. Its genitive ending here is a kasrah.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: It names the action itself.
sections.detail: A noun expressing the action or idea of a verb without tying it to a particular tense.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Writing names the action, without saying who does it or when.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A word built from a verb that describes someone or something doing the action.
sections.detail: A derived noun or adjective denoting the agent or bearer of an action or state.

sections.heading: Related rule
sections.text: This word form is different from the sentence role “subject of the verb”. Learn its meaning in context.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A word naming a person, thing, place or idea.
sections.detail: A noun is a word type; its sentence role and case depend on its use.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: House names a thing. In a sentence it can take different roles and endings.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The noun whose statement inna introduces.
sections.detail: Inna and its sisters make their noun accusative; their predicate is nominative or occupies that position as a phrase or clause.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The student is the noun governed by inna and is accusative.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The information inna gives about its noun.
sections.detail: The predicate of inna is nominative when an inflected single expression; a whole phrase or clause can occupy the nominative predicate position.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Diligent is the predicate of inna; it remains nominative.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A complete verbal clause tells us about the topic.
sections.detail: The verb, its subject and its complements together occupy the nominative predicate position. A pronoun in the clause links it back to the topic.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The complete clause is the predicate, not writes alone; the implicit subject refers back to the student.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A nominal clause tells us about another topic.
sections.detail: The inner topic and predicate form a clause occupying the outer predicate position, with a link back to the outer topic.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: His character is good forms the complete inner nominal clause; his links it to the student.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A predicate that is neither a clause nor a quasi-sentence.
sections.detail: Mufrad here describes structure, not singular number: a dual or plural expression can still be a non-clausal predicate.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Diligent is plural but still a non-clausal predicate.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A prepositional or adverbial expression supplies the predicate.
sections.detail: The whole quasi-sentence occupies the predicate position, traditionally attached to an understood predicate such as situated. A noun inside a prepositional phrase remains genitive.

sections.heading: Example
sections.translation: The student is in the house.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: In the house supplies the location; house alone is not the predicate.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The topic of a nominal sentence placed after its predicate.
sections.detail: A delayed mubtadaʾ follows a fronted predicate; its position does not turn it into the subject of a verb.

sections.heading: Example
sections.translation: There is a man in the house.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: A man is the delayed topic. The location comes first.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The information about a nominal topic placed before that topic.
sections.detail: A fronted khabar precedes the mubtadaʾ. A prepositional or adverbial phrase can occupy this predicate function as a whole.

sections.heading: Example
sections.translation: There is a man in the house.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The complete location phrase is the fronted predicate, not just the noun house.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A connected preposition-and-noun phrase, or an adverbial expression.
sections.detail: A shibh jumla is a prepositional or adverbial phrase. Its sentence function depends on what it relates to; it is not automatically a predicate.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The preposition and its noun form one complete phrase.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A verb used to tell someone to do something.
sections.detail: An imperative verb addresses the listener with a command or request.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The speaker asks the listener to write.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A word that describes a person or thing.
sections.detail: An adjective is a descriptive word type. Its sentence function must be identified separately.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Useful describes the book.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A particle that links words or parts of a sentence.
sections.detail: A coordinating particle links elements; the precise relationship depends on the particle.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Then links the two actions in their order.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A word that points to someone or something.
sections.detail: A demonstrative identifies a referent by pointing, such as this or that.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: This points to the book.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A word such as I, you or he that refers to a person or thing.
sections.detail: A pronoun refers to a participant or a previously identified referent; Arabic uses independent and attached forms.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: I refers to the speaker.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A particle that puts a following imperfect verb in the jussive state.
sections.detail: A jussive particle governs jazm in the relevant imperfect verb; its meaning depends on the particle.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Lam negates the past event and makes the imperfect verb jussive.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A particle that puts a following imperfect verb in the subjunctive state.
sections.detail: Particles such as lan govern naṣb of an imperfect verb. This verb state is distinct from the role of a noun.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Lan negates a future action and makes the imperfect verb subjunctive.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A particle used to introduce a question.
sections.detail: An interrogative particle such as hal introduces a yes/no question.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Hal makes this a yes/no question.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The word that describes a particular noun in this sentence.
sections.detail: As a sentence role, naʿt modifies a noun and normally agrees with it in case, definiteness, gender and number, with agreement rules for non-human plurals.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Useful describes the book and agrees with it.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The noun that an adjective describes.
sections.detail: Manʿūt is the head noun modified by a naʿt; its case comes from its other function in the sentence.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Book is the noun described by useful.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The first noun in a construction such as the door of the house.
sections.detail: The muḍāf is the head of an iḍāfa. Its case depends on its sentence function, and it has no tanwīn in this construction.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Door is the first noun. Its case here does not come from being first in iḍāfa.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The second noun in a construction such as the door of the house.
sections.detail: The muḍāf ilayh specifies the preceding noun in an iḍāfa and is genitive.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: House specifies whose door and is genitive.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The person or thing introduced for the sentence to tell us about.
sections.detail: The mubtadaʾ is the nominal subject or topic; its predicate supplies information about it.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The house is the topic. Big tells us about it.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: What a nominal sentence tells us about its topic.
sections.detail: The khabar supplies the information about the mubtadaʾ; it may be a word, phrase or clause.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Big is what we learn about the house.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The person or thing whose state kāna describes.
sections.detail: The ism of kāna is nominative. Kāna and its sisters affect the case of their predicate.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: The house is the noun of kāna and remains nominative.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: The state or description kāna gives about its noun.
sections.detail: The khabar of kāna is accusative, or a phrase or clause occupying that predicate function.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Big is the predicate of kāna and is accusative here.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.text: A grammatical state of an imperfect verb after certain particles.
sections.detail: Jazm applies to relevant imperfect verbs, never to nouns. Its marker may be sukūn, deletion of nūn or deletion of a weak letter.

sections.heading: Why?
sections.text: Lam makes the imperfect verb jussive. The visible marker here is sukūn.

q_basic.label: Basic Quadriliteral
q_basic.tendency: A basic verb pattern built from four root consonants. Each verb has its own lexical meaning.

q_reflexive.label: Derived Quadriliteral
q_reflexive.tendency: Often expresses a reflexive or resulting action related to the basic quadriliteral verb.

q_infix.label: Quadriliteral n-pattern
q_infix.tendency: Often describes a resulting or intransitive action. Meaning belongs to the particular verb.

q_state.label: Quadriliteral doubled-ending pattern
q_state.tendency: Often describes a state or becoming a certain way. Meaning belongs to the particular verb.
